title: A Wedding at Ecbatana
sum: Raphael brings Tobias to Raguel's house in Ecbatana. Raguel, his wife Edna and their daughter Sarah weep for joy to meet the son of their kinsman Tobit, and grieve to hear that he is blind. Tobias will not eat until Raguel gives him Sarah. Raguel is honest: seven bridegrooms have died on their wedding night. But he gives her anyway, "by the ruling written in the book of Moses," saying that heaven has decided it.

The marriage is made with a spoken formula ("you are her brother and she is your sister") and a written contract, then the meal begins. Edna prepares the bridal room and comforts her frightened daughter: "The Lord of heaven give you gladness instead of your grief." The chapter is full of tears, kisses and blessings, and of the courage of a family that hopes against its own experience.
readings: Read as a patriarch story

The scene is built like Genesis 24 and 29: a young man travels east to his kin, is welcomed with tears and kisses, and receives a bride from her father. Tobit's first readers would hear that the God of Abraham still guides marriages in exile.
Read as a picture of Jewish marriage

The chapter is one of the earliest detailed accounts of a Jewish wedding: a betrothal by the father, a spoken formula, a written contract, a blessing and a feast. It shows customs later laid down in Jewish law, such as the ketubah.

views.C: Catholics read Tobit 7 in the Lectionary as a wedding reading (7:6–14 is among the Old Testament readings offered for the Celebration of Marriage). The Church sees in Raguel's blessing the truth that marriage is God's work before it is a human contract.
views.O: The Orthodox read Tobit as part of the Old Testament from the Septuagint. The chapter's blessings, in which parents commit the couple to God's mercy, fit the Orthodox view of marriage as a holy mystery entered within the family and the church.
views.P: Protestants who read the Apocrypha, such as Anglicans and many Lutherans, value the chapter as an example of a godly marriage arranged with prayer and honesty, while noting that its claim about the law of Moses (7:11–12) has no match in the five books of Moses.
views.H: Scholars note the folk-tale pattern (the dangerous bride, the hero who succeeds where seven failed) and the many links to Genesis. Raguel's appeal to "the book of Moses" shows a diaspora community reading Numbers 36 as a rule for keeping marriage within the family.
views.J: Jewish readers recognize the betrothal, the marriage formula and the written contract as forerunners of the kiddushin and ketubah of later Jewish law. Medieval Hebrew and Aramaic retellings of Tobit kept the scene.

deep.h: Brother, sister and the language of family
deep.b: Almost everyone in this chapter is a "brother" or "sister." Raphael and Tobias call Raguel "our brother," Raguel calls Tobias "brother," and the marriage formula itself turns the couple into "brother" and "sister" (7:11). Raguel even calls his own wife "sister" (7:15). The words belong to a world where marriage joined kin and where the scattered tribes of Israel were one family. The book's first readers, small Jewish communities in foreign cities, were taught to treat one another this way: to welcome the traveler, to keep marriages within the people and to care for each other's poor.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the meal that waits
deep.b: Tobias refuses to eat until the marriage is settled (7:11), and the family eats only after the contract is written (7:14). I suggest the storyteller is echoing Genesis 24:33, where Abraham's servant will not eat until he has told his errand. In both stories the guest's single-minded purpose is a sign that God's plan is at work. Commentators note the Genesis 24 parallels in general; the specific link through the refused meal is my reading.

echoes: Genesis 24:31–51; Genesis 29:11–14; Numbers 36:6–9; Numbers 27:8; Ruth 3:12–13; Ruth 4:1–10; Hosea 2:2; Jeremiah 31:13; Song of Songs 4:9–12

settings.to: Tobias and "Azariah" (Raphael), at Raguel's courtyard door
settings.when: on the travelers' arrival in Ecbatana
settings.why: To show the family's hospitality and grief for Tobit; the recognition scene binds two scattered branches of one family.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. Catholic and Orthodox readers receive it as part of the Old Testament.

settings.to: Tobias, at the evening meal, with Sarah brought in
settings.when: after Tobias refuses to eat until the marriage is settled
settings.why: To tell Tobias the truth about the seven deaths, to give Sarah by the law as Raguel understands it, and to commit the couple to God's protection for the dangerous night.
settings.readers: For them it modeled how a father should marry his daughter within the people and by God's law, honestly and with prayer.
views: Raguel speaks a formula like those in Jewish marriage contracts of the period, so the scene teaches how a marriage is lawfully made.
Raguel gives his daughter knowing seven men have died: the speech shows trust in God's decision ("Heaven has decided," 7:11).

settings.to: her daughter Sarah, in the bridal room
settings.why: To comfort a daughter who had wished to die (3:10–15) and to pray that God would turn her grief into joy.
settings.readers: Mothers and daughters among them would hear a model of faith in God's care when a marriage seemed cursed.

title: The Wedding Night
sum: Tobias does what Raphael told him: he burns the fish's liver and heart, the demon flees to Egypt, and Raphael binds it. Then, before the couple sleep together, Tobias rises and says, "Sister, stand up. Let us pray." His short prayer blesses God, recalls the making of Adam and Eve, and asks for mercy and a long life together. Sarah says Amen.

Outside, Raguel is digging a grave. When the maid finds the couple asleep and alive, Raguel blesses God for his mercy to "two only children," has the grave filled before dawn, and orders a fourteen-day feast. He gives Tobias half of all he owns. Tobias's prayer (8:5–8) became one of the best-known Old Testament texts for Christian weddings, and Jerome's Latin version of the night shaped Catholic teaching on marriage for centuries.
readings: Read as a prayer for married life

Tobias's prayer roots marriage in creation (Genesis 2:18), asks God's mercy rather than relying on the fish, and ends with the simplest wish: to grow old together. Many churches read it at weddings for that reason.
Read as a story of rescue
The night is a battle with a demon that has killed seven men. The fish, the angel and the prayer each have a part; the grave dug and filled in the dark makes the rescue vivid, and a little comic.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary offers Tobit 8:4b–8 as an Old Testament reading at weddings. Catholic teaching sees in it the goods of marriage, the help of the spouses and the gift of children, received with prayer. For centuries the Vulgate's version (three nights of prayer before union, Vulgate 6:16–22; 8:4–5) shaped preaching on chastity in marriage.
views.O: The Orthodox read the chapter from the Septuagint, which has a single night and a single prayer. Its themes, marriage as God's blessing from creation, prayer before married life, and the defeat of the demon, echo the Orthodox service of crowning, which asks God to bless the couple as he blessed the righteous couples of old.
views.P: Protestants value Tobias's prayer as a beautiful model, and Anglican and Lutheran Bibles printed it among the Apocrypha. The first English Prayer Book (1549) even named Raphael's help to Tobias and Sarah in its marriage prayers, a line removed in 1552. Reformed churches give the book no authority.
views.H: Scholars read the episode against folk tales of the "dangerous bride" and ancient exorcism by fumigation. The prayer itself is an early Jewish blessing built on Genesis 2, and the grave-digging scene shows the author's skill with irony.
views.J: Tobias's prayer, opening "Blessed are you, God of our fathers," has the form of later Jewish blessings, and its use of Genesis 2 resembles the seven blessings of the Jewish wedding, which praise God as creator of humankind and of the joy of bride and groom.

deep.h: Three nights or one: the Vulgate's wedding
deep.b:
In the Greek, the couple pray and then sleep together the same night. Jerome's Latin, made from an Aramaic copy (Jerome's preface), tells it differently. Raphael warns that the demon has power over those who marry "to shut out God" and give themselves to lust "as the horse and mule" (Douay 6:17). Tobias must keep apart from Sarah for three nights and pray with her: on the first the demon is driven off, on the second they are admitted to "the society of the holy Patriarchs," on the third they receive the blessing of healthy children (Douay 6:18–21). On the wedding night Tobias says, "for these three nights we are joined to God" (Douay 8:4), and he prays that he takes Sarah "only for the love of posterity" (Douay 8:9).

Because the Vulgate was the Bible of the Western church, this version shaped practice. A rule of the late 400s told newly married couples to keep the first night in continence out of reverence for the wedding blessing (Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua), and medieval and early modern preachers urged "Tobias nights" of prayer before married life. Catholic teaching today imposes no such rule, and modern Catholic translations are made from the Greek.

deep.h: A wedding text across the churches
deep.b: Tobit 8:4b–8 is among the Old Testament readings in the Catholic Lectionary for weddings, and it is often chosen by Catholic couples. The 1549 English Book of Common Prayer asked God to bless the couple "as thou didst send thy angel Raphael to Thobie and Sara," a line later dropped as the Church of England narrowed its use of the Apocrypha. Reformed churches give the Apocrypha no place in public worship.

echoes: Genesis 2:18; Genesis 2:24; Mark 10:6–9; Psalm 128:3–6; Ecclesiastes 9:9; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5; Revelation 20:2; Genesis 29:22–27; Numbers 27:8

settings.to: God, prayed aloud with Sarah in the bridal room
settings.when: after the demon has fled, before the couple sleep together
settings.why: To put the marriage under God's mercy, to ground it in God's making of man and woman, and to ask for a lasting life together; the prayer, not the fish alone, is what Raphael had told them to bring (6:18).
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. It taught them to marry within the faith, for the right reasons and with prayer. Christians have since read it at weddings: the Catholic Lectionary offers 8:4b–8 as a wedding reading.
views: Catholic and many Protestant readers use the prayer as a pattern for Christian couples.
Some readers stress the danger of the night: the prayer asks God to keep them safe from the demon that killed seven men.

settings.to: God, in the house at night
settings.when: when the maid reports that Tobias is alive
settings.why: To give thanks that God turned the feared death into joy and to pray mercy, safety and a joyful life for the young couple.
settings.readers: It showed them how to answer answered prayer: with an immediate blessing of God.

settings.when: the morning after the wedding night
settings.why: To keep Tobias for a fourteen-day feast, to give him half his property, and to adopt him as a son.
settings.readers: Inheritance passing within the family through an heiress's marriage mattered to communities trying to keep their property and identity.

traditions.q: Tobias and Sarah pray before their first night together, and Tobias says he takes her "not for sexual immorality, but in truth" (8:7). What is marriage for, and should a couple's first nights be kept for prayer?
views: Marriage is a sacrament ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children (Catechism 1601, 2363), so the union of husband and wife is good and holy. Tobias's prayer is a model of marrying in God's presence, and 8:4b–8 is a wedding reading. The Vulgate's three nights of continence once shaped custom (a rule of the late 400s asked couples to keep the first night in continence), but the Church imposes no such rule today.

Marriage is a holy mystery in which husband and wife are crowned and journey together toward salvation; children are a blessing of it. The church prays for the couple as God blessed the righteous couples of the Old Testament; Tobit's prayer, like the Vulgate's three nights, is not part of its rite.

Marriage is God's good estate, created in Genesis 2, not a sacrament. Luther taught that marriage is God's work, to be entered with faith and prayer, and he rejected rules that treated married union as less holy. Tobit may be read for its good example, not for doctrine.

The Prayer Book gives three causes of marriage: children, a remedy against sin, and "mutual society, help, and comfort." The 1549 Prayer Book even asked God to bless the couple as he sent Raphael to Tobias and Sarah, a line removed in 1552; Article VI lets the Apocrypha be read "for example of life" only.

Marriage is ordained "for the mutual help of husband and wife, for the increase of mankind," and "for preventing of uncleanness" (Westminster Confession 24.2). Since Tobit is not Scripture, its customs bind no one, and the Vulgate's three nights rest on a text that differs from the Greek.

title: The Money Comes Home
sum: Bound by Raguel's oath to stay for the wedding feast, Tobias sends "Azariah" with four servants and two camels to Rages to collect the silver his father had left with Gabael. Raphael hands over the handwritten document, Gabael counts out the bags with their seals unbroken, and the two travel back together to the wedding.

Gabael weeps when he sees Tobias and blesses him in the same words Raguel used: son of a fine and good man, righteous and a giver of alms. The short chapter ties off the errand that began the journey (4:1–2; 5:1–3): the money was the reason for the trip, but a wife and a healing are what God had in store.

views.C: Catholic readers see in Gabael the faithful steward and in the errand an image of providence: the journey Tobit planned for money becomes the means of the blessings he could not plan.
views.O: The Orthodox read the chapter as part of the story of God's hidden care, carried out through an angel who serves quietly as a hired companion.
views.P: Protestant readers of the Apocrypha value Gabael's honesty and Tobias's respect for an oath as examples of godly conduct.
views.H: The chapter shows the economic life of diaspora Jews: deposits, signed bonds, trust between kin across great distances. Scholars note that the geography (Ecbatana to Rages and back in a few days) is unrealistic, one of several signs that the book is a story, not a travel record.
views.J: The trust between Tobit and Gabael reflects Jewish networks of kinship and credit across the eastern diaspora, which later Jewish law would regulate in detail.

settings.to: Raphael, whom he knows as "Brother Azariah"
settings.why: To finish his father's errand without breaking Raguel's oath, while sparing his father worry.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. It showed a son keeping both an oath and his duty to his parents.

settings.why: To honor Tobit through his son and to ask heaven's blessing on the whole family.
settings.readers: The good name of a righteous, generous father was a blessing for his children.

title: A Mother Watches the Road
sum: In Nineveh, Tobit counts the days and begins to fear the worst. Anna is sure her son is dead: "Woe is me, my child! I let you go, you, the light of my eyes." Tobit tries to comfort her, unaware of how truly he speaks: the man with their son can be trusted. Anna watches the road every day and weeps every night.

In Ecbatana, when the fourteen days end, Tobias insists on going home. Raguel gives him Sarah and half his wealth, and he and Edna send them off with blessings. Edna entrusts her daughter to Tobias "before the Lord" as a precious deposit. Tobias leaves blessing "the Lord of heaven and earth, the King of all."

views.C: Catholic readers value the chapter's portrait of family love and of in-laws who become parents. Edna's entrusting of her daughter "before the Lord" has been used in Catholic marriage preparation as an image of the bride entrusted to the husband's care.
views.O: The Orthodox read Anna's grief and Raguel's blessings as part of the book's teaching that God hears the prayers and tears of families.
views.P: Protestant readers find in Anna an honest picture of anxiety, and in Tobit a model, imperfect but real, of trust that God is caring for those far away.
views.H: Scholars point to the storyteller's craft: parallel scenes in two cities, dramatic irony, and the emotional realism of Anna, one of the book's most vivid characters. The two Greek forms differ much in this chapter.
views.J: Anna's watch for her son and Raguel's blessings reflect the warmth of Jewish family life; the parents' blessing of children before a journey remains a Jewish custom.

echoes: Psalm 38:10; Genesis 24:55–60; Ruth 1:16–17; 1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:12; Exodus 20:12

settings.to: each other, at home in Nineveh
settings.when: after the expected days of the journey have passed
settings.why: Anna voices a mother's despair; Tobit tries to calm her with trust in the trustworthy guide.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. Parents who sent children on long journeys, or lost them, would hear their own fear named and answered by the story's outcome.

settings.when: after Tobias asks to leave (end of 10:7), when the fourteen days of the feast are over
settings.why: Raguel offers to send messengers; Tobias insists on going home to parents who think him dead, a son's loyalty overriding his host's wishes.
settings.readers: It showed that a new marriage does not cancel duty to one's parents.

settings.when: as they set out for Nineveh
settings.why: To send the couple off under God's protection, to make Tobias their son and Sarah his parents' daughter, and to entrust Sarah to her husband's care.
settings.readers: It modeled the blessing of a departing bride and the joining of two families.

title: Tobit Sees Again
sum: Near Nineveh, Raphael and Tobias hurry ahead of Sarah. Anna sees her son coming and runs to him: "I have seen you, my child. From now on I can die." Tobit stumbles out to meet him. Tobias blows into his father's eyes, applies the fish's gall, and peels the white films away. Tobit sees his son and bursts into praise: blessed be God, his great name and all his holy angels, "He struck me, and look, I see my son Tobias!"

Tobit walks unaided to the city gate to welcome Sarah, and all Nineveh is amazed. He blesses his new daughter and her God, and there is joy among all the Jews of Nineveh. Ahiqar and Nadab come to share it, and the wedding is celebrated again for seven days.
readings: Read as a healing story
God heals through a remedy and a son's hands, guided by an angel's knowledge; the healing is public, so that Tobit can give thanks before everyone (11:17; 12:6).
Read as a picture of return

A son thought dead comes home, a blind man sees, a bride is welcomed: Christian readers have seen in it the joy of the lost son's homecoming (Luke 15:20–24), and Jewish readers the hope of exiles' return.

views.C: Catholic tradition reads Tobit's healing as God's mercy after trial ("he struck me," 11:15) and has used the scene in art and preaching on the healing power of God and the intercession of Raphael, patron of the sick and of travelers.
views.O: The Orthodox read the healing as God's work through his angel, in keeping with the church's prayers for healing and its honor of the archangels.
views.P: Protestant readers value Tobit's praise as a model of thanksgiving, while holding that the book's angelology and remedies teach no doctrine.
views.H: Scholars note the medical realism (leucoma, gall in eye salves) and the folk-tale motif of the helper's remedy. The hymn of 11:14–15 anticipates the full hymn of chapter 13.
views.J: Tobit's blessing of God's "great name" and his angels reflects Jewish piety of the Second Temple period. The phrase "May his great name rest on us" resembles the later Kaddish prayer's praise of God's great name.

echoes: Genesis 46:30; Luke 15:20–24; Luke 2:29–30; John 9:6–7; Mark 8:23–25; Genesis 2:7; Deuteronomy 32:39; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–6; Psalm 103:20–21

settings.why: To prepare the healing and the homecoming.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. It assured them that God provides the means of help, not only the result.

settings.what: Tobit's blessing when he sees again
settings.when: the moment the white films are peeled away
settings.why: To bless God, his name and his angels, and to confess that the God who struck him has now healed him.
settings.readers: For readers who suffered in exile it modeled praise that names both God's discipline and his mercy.
views: The words are a spontaneous blessing for one man's healing.
Many read it as the first line of chapter 13: what God does for Tobit he will do for Israel (13:2, 13:5).

settings.to: Sarah, at the gate of Nineveh
settings.why: To bless the bride, her God and her father, and to welcome her into her new home.
settings.readers: It showed a new daughter-in-law welcomed with honor and joy.

title: I Am Raphael
sum: When the feast is over, Tobit and Tobias want to pay their guide well: half of everything he brought back. Instead, "Azariah" takes them aside and teaches them: bless God, thank him before everyone alive, and tell what he has done. Prayer with truth and alms with righteousness are better than wealth with wrongdoing; alms rescue from death and cleanse away every sin.

Then he reveals himself. He carried the memorial of their prayers before God's glory, he was sent to test Tobit and to heal him and Sarah, and he is Raphael, "one of the seven angels who stand in attendance" before the Lord. They fall on their faces in fear. Raphael tells them not to fear, to bless God, and to write everything down. He never really ate; they saw a vision. Then he goes up, and they see him no more.
readings: Read as the key to the story
The revelation explains everything before it: the prayers heard in 3:16–17, the 'good angel' of 5:22, the fish and the remedy. The reader, who knew the secret, now watches the characters learn it.
Read as teaching
Raphael's speech (12:6–10) gathers the book's message, thanksgiving, prayer, alms and righteousness, into a short sermon, much like the farewell speeches of the Bible.

views.C: The Catholic Church honors Raphael as an archangel named in Scripture (feast of Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, 29 September). It reads 12:12 and 12:15 as witness that angels present prayers to God (Catechism 334–336) and 12:8–9 as teaching on the value of almsgiving with prayer and fasting (Catechism 1434). The Vulgate's line "because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee" is classic in Catholic spiritual writing.
views.O: The Orthodox honor Raphael among the seven archangels at the Synaxis of the Archangels (8 November) and read the chapter as a witness to the angels' service in presenting prayers and in healing.
views.P: Protestants read the chapter as the Apocrypha, not as doctrine. Lutheran and Reformed teachers objected to 12:9 (alms that cleanse sin) as contrary to justification by faith (Apology of the Augsburg Confession, article 4), and the Reformed writer William Whitaker to the angel's assumed name (5:13).
views.H: Scholars see a carefully staged revelation scene like Judges 13 and the later Gospel scenes. The seven angels reflect Jewish angel lore of the 200s BC (1 Enoch 20). The command to write (12:20) presents the book as an eyewitness record.
views.J: Jewish tradition kept Raphael as one of the four angels around God's throne (Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, Raphael) and as the angel of healing. The idea that angels bring prayers before God is found in later rabbinic and mystical writings as well.

deep.b:
Raphael is "one of the seven angels who stand in attendance" before the Lord (12:15). Revelation knows the same seven: "the seven angels who stand in God's presence" receive seven trumpets (Revelation 8:2), and then "another angel" offers incense "along with the prayers of all God's people" on the golden altar (Revelation 8:3). The shorter Greek of Tobit makes the link even closer: the seven "present the prayers of the saints" (see the variant). Gabriel tells Zechariah that he is "the one who stands before God" (Luke 1:19). Whether John knew Tobit cannot be proved; both draw on Jewish lore of seven chief angels, which 1 Enoch 20 lists by name.

For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, Tobit 12 is part of the scriptural basis for honoring angels and asking their help; for Protestants, Revelation 8 shows the prayers rising, but not that believers should address angels. The question whether angels carry our prayers is carded at 1 Enoch 99, and the honor of angels named outside the 66 books at 1 Enoch 20.

Raphael repeats Tobit's teaching of 4:7–11: alms "rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (12:9). Cyprian of Carthage quoted these verses in On Works and Almsgiving to urge Christians to give: alms, he said, heal the wounds of sins committed after baptism. Catholic teaching places almsgiving with prayer and fasting among the works of penance that express conversion and obtain mercy (Catechism 1434, 2447), always by God's grace. Melanchthon's Apology of the Augsburg Confession (article 4) answered that such texts describe the fruits of faith, which God rewards, and must not be read as if works earn forgiveness, which comes by faith in Christ alone. The churches' views are set side by side in the card at 4:10.

echoes: Revelation 8:2–4; Luke 1:19; Acts 10:4; Judges 13:15–20; Genesis 18:8; Revelation 22:8–9; John 16:5; Matthew 6:1–21; Luke 11:41; Proverbs 10:2; Daniel 4:27; 1 John 1:7; Genesis 22:1

settings.when: after the wedding feast in Nineveh
settings.why: To pay the hired guide generously: father and son agree on half of everything he brought back, a reward that sets up the angel's refusal and revelation.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. Paying a worker's wages promptly and fully was a command of the law (Deuteronomy 24:14–15) and of Tobit's own teaching (4:14).

settings.what: Raphael's teaching on thanksgiving and alms
settings.when: when they offer to pay him half of the goods
settings.why: To turn their gratitude from him to God, and to sum up the life that pleases God: open thanksgiving, true prayer, generous alms and righteousness.
settings.readers: Without a Temple nearby, prayer and almsgiving were the center of their religious life; the speech assured them these were worth more than wealth and could even save from death.
views: The speech is wisdom teaching like Proverbs and Sirach.
Catholic readers have taken 12:9 as teaching that alms help to cleanse sin; Lutheran and Reformed readers reject that reading (see the card at 4:10).

settings.when: after the teaching, before he departs
settings.why: To reveal that God heard their prayers and saw their good deeds, that God sent the angel, and that everything should now be written down and told.
settings.readers: The scene assured scattered Jews that their prayers reached God's presence and that God's messengers were at work unseen in ordinary lives.
views: Catholic and Orthodox readers receive the scene as Scripture's witness to a real angel and his service.
Historical critics read it as the climax of an edifying story, shaped like Judges 13.

traditions.q: Raphael called himself "Azariah, son of the great Hananiah" (5:13), and let the family think he ate with them, though "you were seeing a vision" (12:19). Did the angel deceive them? (Whether a lie can ever be right is asked at Joshua 2, about Rahab; this card asks only about an angel in human form.)
views: Thomas Aquinas holds that angels may take on bodies, and that "it is not contrary to the truth of the holy angels" that in them they appear as living men, since they show themselves so to point to spiritual things. Of Raphael's meals he says, quoting Tobit 12:19, that this was "not a true eating, but figurative of spiritual eating" (Summa I q.51 a.3, replies 1 and 5). Catholic commentators (Challoner, Calmet, Menochius, as gathered by Haydock) add that the angel had taken the form of Azariah and could use his name, and that the names fit his errand: Azariah means "the help of God," Hananiah "the grace of God."

William Whitaker, in his Disputation on Holy Scripture against the Catholic canon, "would have this to be a lie" (so Haydock reports him): a holy angel who says he is a man of a named family says what is false, and that is one of his reasons for denying that Tobit is Scripture.

title: Tobit's Song for Jerusalem
sum: Tobit answers the angel with a psalm. Its first half praises the God who "strikes, and he shows mercy": he scattered Israel among the nations, and there Israel must thank him; if they turn back with all their heart, he will turn back to them and gather them. Its second half turns to Jerusalem: the city will be struck for its children's sins, but its tent will be rebuilt with joy.

Then comes a vision of glory. A bright light shines to the ends of the earth, nations come with gifts, those who love Jerusalem are happy, and the city is rebuilt with gates of sapphire and emerald, towers of gold and streets of red gems, while every house cries "Hallelujah!" Christians have long read the song beside Revelation 21's new Jerusalem. Codex Sinaiticus lacks 13:6b–10a; the Plain English Translation fills the gap from Vaticanus.
readings: Read as Israel's hope
The song moves from one family's story to the nation's: Tobit's blindness and healing become a picture of exile and return, and the book's private joy becomes the joy of Jerusalem.
Read with Revelation 21

The jeweled city, the nations bringing gifts and the Hallelujah all return in Revelation 21–22 and 19. Christians read Tobit's hope as fulfilled in the heavenly city; others read it as a still-future earthly restoration.

views.C: Catholic tradition prays the song in the Liturgy of the Hours as Old Testament canticles (13:1–8 and 13:8–11, 13–15). It keeps the literal sense, Jerusalem rebuilt after the exile, and adds a spiritual sense in which the city is a figure of the Church, "the holy city" of the end (Catechism 1045).
views.O: The Orthodox read the hymn as prophecy fulfilled in the Church, the new Jerusalem, and completed in the age to come, when God will dwell with his people.
views.P: Protestant readers value the hymn as a beautiful Jewish witness to the hope the prophets and Revelation share, but do not use it to establish doctrine. Many Reformed and Lutheran interpreters read Revelation 21 of the renewed creation and God's people, with Tobit as background.
views.H: Scholars read chapter 13 as a psalm built from Isaiah 54 and 60, Deuteronomy 30 and the Psalms of Zion, written before the Maccabean crisis of 167 BC. The Qumran fragments include parts of it, as reported by Fitzmyer, so it belonged to the book's oldest known form.
views.J: The song is close to Jewish prayers for the ingathering of exiles and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, such as the blessings of the Amidah. Its jeweled city also appears in the Aramaic New Jerusalem texts from Qumran and later rabbinic legend.

deep.h: Tobit 13 and Revelation 21 side by side
deep.b:
Shared: gates and walls of precious stone (13:16; Revelation 21:18–21); gold (13:16; Revelation 21:18, 21); the nations bringing gifts and walking in the city's light (13:11; Revelation 21:24–26); the hallelujah of the redeemed (13:18; Revelation 19:1–6); joy that replaces mourning (13:14; Revelation 21:4). Both draw on Isaiah 54:11–12 and Isaiah 60.

Different: Tobit's city is the earthly Jerusalem rebuilt after exile, with God's house inside it (13:16; 14:5) and the exiles gathered back to the land (13:13; 14:7). John's city comes "down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:2), there is no temple in it because God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:22), and it stands in a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1). Whether John used Tobit is debated; the shared images suggest at least a common tradition of Jewish hope.

deep.h: An earthly Jerusalem, or the Church?
deep.b: Tobit hopes for a rebuilt Jerusalem on earth, with God's house in it and the exiles gathered back to the land (13:9–18; 14:5–7). Christians read that hope in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox tradition keeps the literal sense, the city's rebuilding after the exile, and sees its fullest meaning in the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem: the Liturgy of the Hours prays the song as a canticle of thanksgiving for the people's deliverance. Reformed interpreters read such prophecies as fulfilled in Christ and his people and finally in the new earth (Hoekema). Dispensationalists expect a literal restored Jerusalem at the center of Christ's thousand-year kingdom (Ryrie). The site asks these questions where the 66 books raise them: on the thousand years at Revelation 20 and Psalm 72, and on the land promised to Israel at Numbers 34 and Joshua 21.

Sinaiticus breaks off in the middle of 13:6 and resumes in the middle of 13:10, with "your tent" addressed to a Jerusalem the surviving text has not named. Swete prints the gap and gives the Vaticanus text, and the Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus for the missing lines (13:6b–10a), marked in the variants. The lines include Tobit's appeal to sinners ("who knows whether he will want you and show you mercy?") and the address "Jerusalem, city of the Holy One."

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; Isaiah 54:11–12; Isaiah 60:1–14; Isaiah 66:10; Psalm 48:2; Psalm 122:6; Psalm 103:1; Amos 9:11; Revelation 21:1–27; Revelation 19:1–6; Matthew 5:4; Matthew 6:9

settings.to: God, and through the hymn the Israelites scattered among the nations, and Jerusalem itself
settings.when: after Raphael's departure; Vaticanus says Tobit "wrote a prayer of rejoicing"
settings.why: To turn one family's rescue into a promise for the whole people: the God who struck and healed Tobit will punish and then gather Israel, and will rebuild Jerusalem in glory.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. Living among the nations, they heard that their exile had a purpose (to make God known, 13:3–4), that turning back to God would bring him back to them, and that Jerusalem's glory was still ahead. Christians later read the song with Revelation 21.
views: Most scholars: written for scattered Jews who prayed for the gathering of exiles.
Catholic and Orthodox tradition also reads the rebuilt city as a figure of the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem.

title: Tobit's Last Words
sum: Tobit dies at a great age, after a life of good times and alms. Before he dies he calls Tobias and gives his testament. He believes God's word through Nahum: Nineveh will fall. Tobias must take his family to Media. Tobit foretells the exile of Judah, the burning of the Temple, the return, a lesser second Temple, and then a glorious Jerusalem, the gathering of all Israel and the nations' turning from idols to God.

His last teaching is about alms and wrongdoing. Nadab tried to kill Ahiqar, the uncle who raised him, but Ahiqar's alms saved him from the death trap and Nadab fell into it: "see what alms do, and what wrongdoing does: it kills." Tobias buries his parents, moves to Ecbatana, cares for Raguel and Edna, and dies at 117, after rejoicing at the news of Nineveh's fall.
readings: Read as a farewell testament
Like Jacob (Genesis 49), Moses (Deuteronomy 31–33) and David (1 Kings 2), Tobit gathers his family before death, foretells the future and gives his last commands.
Read as history told as prophecy
Tobit, set in the 700s BC, foretells events up to about 500 BC accurately, then a still-future glory. Many scholars read this as the author's own vantage point around 200 BC.

views.C: Catholic readers receive Tobit's testament as inspired teaching on fidelity, almsgiving and hope, and note that Catholic teaching allows for the literary form of such prophecies (Dei Verbum 12). The book's ending, with honored burials and long lives, is read as God's blessing on the just.
views.O: The Orthodox read the chapter as prophecy of Israel's return and of the nations' conversion, fulfilled in Christ's Church.
views.P: Protestant readers note that 14:4 has a famous textual difference (Nahum in Sinaiticus, Jonah in Vaticanus and the KJV) and use the chapter as historical background to the Second Temple period, not as doctrine.
views.H: Most scholars date the book by this chapter: it knows the return from exile and the modest Second Temple, but not the desecration of 167 BC or the Maccabean revolt, so it was likely written around 225–175 BC. The Ahiqar story shows the author drawing on international wisdom literature.
views.J: The testament's hopes, the ingathering of exiles, a glorious Jerusalem and a new Temple, are central to Jewish prayer. The Ahiqar tale it cites was widely known among Jews, as the Elephantine papyrus shows.

deep.b: In 14:4 Sinaiticus says Tobit believes "the things Nahum spoke" about Nineveh; Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, says "what Jonah the prophet spoke," and repeats Jonah in 14:8. The difference matters for reading the Bible: in the book of Jonah, God spares Nineveh when it repents (Jonah 3:10; 4:11), so Jonah's "forty days" did not come true, while Nahum's entire book announces the fall that happened in 612 BC. Most modern commentators therefore read Nahum. The Jonah reading is old, however, and Josephus also links Jonah with a prophecy of Nineveh's fall, which shows that Jews could read Jonah's warning as only postponed. Both readings agree that God's word against a violent empire stands.

echoes: Nahum 1:1; Nahum 3:7; Nahum 3:19; Zephaniah 2:13–15; Jonah 3:4–10; Jonah 4:11; 2 Kings 25:9; Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3–9; Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23; Deuteronomy 30:19; Genesis 49:1–33

settings.when: as Tobit is dying in Nineveh
settings.why: To send his family to safety before Nineveh falls, to assure them that every word of the prophets will come true (exile, return, glory), and to leave them his rule of life: serve God in truth, give alms, do what is right.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews of the diaspora around 200 BC, a minority under Greek kings far from Jerusalem, who kept the law, married within the community and helped one another without a Temple nearby. They lived in the time after the "lesser" Temple of 14:5 and before the hoped-for glory; the testament told them where they stood in God's plan and how to live while they waited.
views: Catholic and Orthodox readers receive the testament as inspired; many also allow that its form may be history told as prophecy.
Most historians: the author, writing around 200 BC, put known history in Tobit's mouth to make the still-future hope credible.
